title: Oil Posts 5% Weekly Drop Despite Tanker Attacks, Saudi Arabia Expands Storage in Japan, and US Senate Clears Permitting Reform
subhead: Brent crude tumbled toward $91–$92 a barrel on looming supply surplus forecasts even as Houthi missile threats and tanker attacks persisted in the Middle East, while Saudi Arabia struck a crude storage deal with Japan and the US Senate passed major energy permitting legislation.

sections.heading: Oil Drops 5% on Surplus Forecasts Despite Tanker Attacks and Yemen Strikes
sections.body:
Brent crude tumbled 5% this week toward $91 to $92.18 per barrel as forecasts of an upcoming supply glut and steady Gulf flows to Asia outweighed ongoing tanker attacks and Middle East tensions, OilPrice and Anadolu Agency report. Baker Hughes data cited by OilPrice also showed active US oil and gas drilling rigs climbed to 607, up 53 from a year earlier.

On the security front, Times of Israel reports that the Saudi-led coalition intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles heading toward Riyadh while the US Treasury sanctioned Iranian 'trustees' collecting illicit oil revenues, and Anadolu Agency notes the UN warned that Saudi-led strikes on Yemen's Port of Hudaydah threaten vital aid lifelines. Meanwhile, TRT World reports Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is open to diplomacy but insists enriched uranium must remain inside Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: Oil markets are currently pricing physical oversupply over geopolitical risk premiums, leaving crude benchmarks insulated unless Gulf export infrastructure suffers direct disruption.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Expands Oil Storage in Japan as Tokyo Restocks Petroleum Reserves
sections.body:
Japan plans to purchase up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to replenish national petroleum reserves drawn down during the Strait of Hormuz crisis, under a Friday agreement making purchases contingent on favorable market conditions, OilPrice reports. Tokyo had tapped its strategic stockpiles earlier to cushion domestic refiners from Middle East shipping disruptions.

As part of the bilateral arrangement, Tokyo granted Saudi Arabia temporary use of an additional 16 million barrels of commercial crude storage capacity in Japan. Separately, SCMP notes that Japan has been floating an Asian energy agency to coordinate emergency supplies, though regional neighbors have yet to commit despite existing unused oil-sharing pacts.
sections.whyItMatters: Expanding Saudi crude storage inside Japan gives Riyadh forward-positioned supply for Asian buyers while helping Tokyo rebuild strategic buffers against future Strait of Hormuz disruptions.

sections.heading: US Senate Passes Permitting Reform Bill as States Target Data Center Power Costs
sections.body:
The US Senate approved a major permitting reform bill aimed at accelerating the build-out of domestic energy production and transmission infrastructure, clearing a key legislative hurdle toward becoming law, The Hill reports.

At the state level, OilPrice notes that incoming Democratic governors starting in January will lead states holding 77% of the 300 GW in US data center capacity announced for 2027–2030—including Texas, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Georgia—after campaigning to force hyperscalers to pay their full grid costs. Meanwhile, a separate OilPrice analysis notes that Democratic control of both chambers of Congress in January will intensify federal energy policy battles.
sections.whyItMatters: Federal permitting reform could speed up power transmission, but state-level backlash over data center electricity bills threatens to raise operating costs for US AI infrastructure.

sections.heading: Lufthansa Cuts 1,000 Jobs Over Fuel Costs; US Pushes Pure Lithium Takeover
sections.body:
Europe's largest airline group, Lufthansa, plans to eliminate up to 1,000 jobs and trim short- and medium-haul capacity as soaring jet fuel prices squeeze carrier profitability, OilPrice reports citing Bloomberg.

In critical minerals, Reuters exclusively reports that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urged battery startup Pure Lithium to accept a US government-backed takeover, according to documents and a source familiar with the talks. Separately, OilPrice reports that Argentine energy firms are rushing to issue bonds ahead of the 2027 election as Vaca Muerta shale exports surge.
sections.whyItMatters: High refined fuel costs are forcing European aviation capacity cuts even as crude drops, while Washington's push into battery startups reflects direct state intervention in lithium supply chains.

sections.heading: COP31 Closes With Contested Transition Language; Wood Mackenzie Sees EV Boost
sections.body:
United Nations climate negotiations at COP31 ran into deadlock over fossil fuels' role in Africa's energy transition, with nations struggling to finalize a climate plan as the summit closed in Antalya, Mongabay and Al Jazeera report, leaving financing targets unresolved.

Looking at long-term demand, ET Auto reports Wood Mackenzie's assessment that recent oil price shocks and high retail fuel costs are set to accelerate global electric vehicle adoption, while Automotive News highlights the US auto sector's strategic dilemma between relying on foreign oil or Chinese battery supply chains.
sections.whyItMatters: Deadlock at COP31 leaves developing economies without clear transition financing rules, reinforcing market-driven shifts toward EVs where fuel prices remain elevated.

bottomLine: A 5% weekly slide in Brent crude shows ample Middle Eastern supply flows currently outweighing tanker attacks and Riyadh missile interceptions, while Saudi Arabia's expanded storage deal in Japan and US Senate permitting reform reshape physical buffers and grid build-out rules.
sources: OilPrice, Anadolu Agency, Times of Israel, TRT World, SCMP, The Hill, Reuters, Mongabay, Al Jazeera, ET Auto, Automotive News
